lesson.goal: load a CSV with pandas, then select, filter, clean and group the data

sources.title: Learn Pandas in 30 Minutes: Load, Select, Filter, Clean and Group a CSV

steps.title: Install pandas and load orders.csv
steps.instructions: Run `uv init .` and `uv add pandas`, download orders.csv from https://github.com/techwithtim/PanadasTutorial into the folder, then in main.py read it with `pd.read_csv('orders.csv')` and print it. Run `uv run main.py` to see the rows x columns summary.

targets.caption: Import pandas with the conventional pd alias
Load orders.csv into a DataFrame
Printed DataFrame summary: rows x columns

explanations.topic: Installing pandas with pip / pip3
Using uv to create a virtual environment and add pandas
Why import pandas as pd
DataFrame vs Series
CSV files and two-dimensional data
pd.read_csv loads a CSV into a DataFrame
Reading the printed DataFrame (rows x columns)

hints: Make sure pandas is installed: `uv add pandas` inside a uv project, or `pip install pandas` (`pip3` on Mac/Linux).
Put orders.csv in the same folder as main.py; download it from the GitHub repo linked in the description.
main.py needs three lines: `import pandas as pd`, `df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv')`, `print(df)`.
Run it with `uv run main.py` (or `python main.py`); the output should end with `[40 rows x 9 columns]`.
common_mistakes: Running `python main.py` outside the uv environment, giving `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas'`.
orders.csv not in the working directory, causing `FileNotFoundError`.
Typing `pd.readcsv` or `pd.read_CSV` instead of `pd.read_csv`.
Using `pip install` on Mac/Linux where only `pip3` points to Python 3.
Forgetting `print(df)` in a .py file, so nothing appears in the terminal.

steps.title: Load data in a Jupyter notebook
steps.instructions: Create notebook.ipynb and in the first cell import pandas and load orders.csv with pd.read_csv. In a second cell run `print(df)`.

targets.caption: First cell: import pandas and load orders.csv
Second cell: print the DataFrame

explanations.topic: Why use a Jupyter notebook instead of a .py file for pandas
Opening a new Jupyter notebook via Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P
Installing the VS Code Python extension for notebook support
Notebook cells run independently; the loaded df persists between cells
Running cells, execute above/below, deleting cells, clearing outputs

hints: Press Ctrl+Shift+P (Cmd+Shift+P on Mac), type "New Jupyter Notebook", and save the file as notebook.ipynb in the same folder as orders.csv.
In the first cell, write import pandas as pd and then df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv'), then click the run button next to the cell.
When asked, choose the Python interpreter or kernel that has pandas installed.
Add a second cell below with print(df) and run only that cell. The DataFrame should appear under it.
common_mistakes: Saving the notebook in a different folder from orders.csv, which causes FileNotFoundError.
Picking a kernel or interpreter where pandas isn't installed, which causes ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas'.
Running the print(df) cell before the read_csv cell, which causes NameError: name 'df' is not defined.
Not having the VS Code Python/Jupyter extension, so "New Jupyter Notebook" doesn't appear in the command palette.
Writing pd.readcsv instead of pd.read_csv.
steps.run_command: Run Cell 1, then Run Cell 2 (select a Python kernel when prompted)

steps.title: Explore the DataFrame
steps.instructions: In separate cells run `df.head()`, `df.tail()`, `df.info()`, `df.describe()`, `df.columns` and `df.index`. Check that info reports 40 entries and 9 columns.

targets.caption: info() prints row count, column count and dtypes
describe() gives summary statistics
index shows the RangeIndex

explanations.topic: head() shows the first five rows
tail() shows the last five rows
info() lists entries, columns and dtypes
Why text columns show as object dtype
describe() generates descriptive statistics
columns lists the column names
index is a RangeIndex: start 0, stop 40, step 1

hints: Put each call in its own cell and run it with Shift+Enter so each output appears under its cell.
info() and describe() are methods, so they need parentheses. columns and index are attributes, so they don't.
In the info() output, look for 'RangeIndex: 40 entries' and 'Data columns (total 9 columns)'. If those numbers differ, check that you loaded the full orders.csv.
Run the cell that loads the CSV into df before running these cells, otherwise df is undefined.
common_mistakes: Calling df.columns() or df.index(), which raises TypeError because they are attributes, not methods.
Writing df.info without parentheses, which prints the bound method instead of the summary.
Running the exploration cells before the cell that creates df (NameError: name 'df' is not defined).
Expecting describe() to summarise every column; by default it only covers the numeric ones.
Loading the wrong or a partial CSV, so info doesn't report 40 entries and 9 columns.
steps.run_command: Run each cell in the Jupyter notebook (Shift+Enter)

steps.title: Select columns and rows
steps.instructions: Select a single column with `df['Country']` and multiple with `df[['Country', 'Product']]`. Select rows by position with `df.iloc[0]` and `df.iloc[10]['Country']`.

targets.caption: Select a row by position with iloc
Pass a list of column names to get a DataFrame

explanations.topic: Single-column indexing returns a pandas Series
Using Python built-ins like len() and set() on a Series
A list of columns returns a new DataFrame, not a Series
iloc selects rows by integer position
A row can be accessed by index position or by column name

hints: Start by running df.columns so you can see the exact column names.
For one column use df['ColumnName']. For several columns, put a list inside the brackets: df[['A', 'B']].
For rows, use df.iloc[n] with square brackets, not parentheses.
Chain a column lookup onto a row: df.iloc[10]['Country'].
common_mistakes: Using single brackets with two names, e.g. df['Country', 'Product'], which raises a KeyError. Use df[['Country', 'Product']] instead.
Writing df.iloc(0) with parentheses instead of df.iloc[0].
Mistyping or miscasing a column name (e.g. 'country' vs 'Country'), which causes a KeyError.
Using an iloc index of 40 or higher on a 40-row DataFrame, which causes an IndexError.

steps.title: Filter rows with boolean conditions
steps.instructions: Filter with `df[df['Category'] == 'Electronics']`, combine conditions with `&` and `|` in parentheses. Try numeric filters like `df[df['Quantity'] > 2]`.

targets.caption: Filter rows with a boolean condition
Combine parenthesized conditions with & or |

explanations.topic: Boolean indexing: df[condition] keeps rows where the condition is True
Empty result from filtering the wrong column (Product vs Category)
Combine conditions with single & inside parentheses, not Python's 'and'
Use single | for OR conditions
Numeric comparisons >, <, <=, != in filters

hints: Wrap a comparison on a column inside df[...]: df[df['Category'] == 'Electronics'].
To combine conditions, put each one in parentheses and join with & (and) or | (or).
Example: df[(df['Category'] == 'Electronics') & (df['Country'] == 'USA')].
For numbers, compare directly: df[df['Quantity'] > 2].
common_mistakes: Filtering the wrong column (e.g. 'Product' instead of 'Category') and getting an empty table
Using Python's 'and'/'or' instead of & and |, which raises 'The truth value of a Series is ambiguous'
Forgetting parentheses around each condition when using & or |
Column name case/spelling mismatch causing a KeyError
Comparing a string column to a number or wrong capitalization like 'electronics'

steps.title: Use string and isin filters
steps.instructions: Filter names with `.str.startswith('A')` and `.str.endswith('a')` on the customer name column. Use `.isin([...])` on Country and negate it with `~`.

targets.caption: String method filter on names
Filter rows by a list of countries

explanations.topic: str.startswith gives a boolean mask of names starting with a letter
String matching is case-sensitive, so endswith('A') returns nothing
.str accessor exposes string methods on a column
isin replaces a long chain of combined OR conditions
~ reverses a boolean condition (NOT in the list)

hints: String methods on a column are reached through the .str accessor, e.g. df['CustomerName'].str...
Wrap the condition in df[...] so it filters rows: df[df['CustomerName'].str.startswith('A')].
isin takes a list: df[df['Country'].isin(['USA', 'Sweden', 'Brazil'])].
To negate, put ~ in front of the whole condition: df[~df['Country'].isin([...])].
common_mistakes: Using endswith('A') with an uppercase letter and getting an empty result, because matching is case-sensitive.
Calling df['CustomerName'].startswith('A') without .str, which raises AttributeError.
Passing separate arguments to isin, as in isin('USA', 'Sweden'), instead of one list.
Putting ~ inside the list or using `not`/`!` instead of ~ in front of the boolean mask.
Misspelling column names such as 'Customer Name' or 'country', which causes a KeyError.

steps.title: Update and delete rows
steps.instructions: Update values with `df.loc[df['Country'] == 'USA', 'Country'] = 'United States'` and uppercase with `df['Country'] = df['Country'].str.upper()`. Delete a row with `df = df.drop(39)` and confirm with `df.tail()`.

targets.caption: Locate rows and assign a new value
Uppercase the Country column
Drop a row and reassign df

explanations.topic: loc locates by label/condition vs iloc by position
loc with a condition returns a DataFrame (possibly multiple rows)
loc[condition, column] = value updates matching rows
Bulk update all USA entries to United States
Vectorized string methods via .str.upper()
drop removes a row by index label; reassign to keep it

hints: Use df.loc[<condition>, '<column>'] = <new value> to update only the rows matching a condition.
The condition is a boolean Series like df['Country'] == 'USA'; the column name goes after the comma.
For a whole column, assign back: df['Country'] = df['Country'].str.upper().
df.drop(39) returns a new DataFrame, so write df = df.drop(39), then check with df.tail().
common_mistakes: Chained assignment like df[df['Country']=='USA']['Country'] = 'United States', which doesn't update df (SettingWithCopyWarning).
Using .upper() directly on the Series instead of .str.upper(), causing AttributeError.
Calling df.drop(39) without reassigning, so the row is still there in df.tail().
Running df.drop(39) twice, giving KeyError: '[39] not found in axis'.
Misspelling the column name (e.g. 'Product Name' vs 'Product'), which silently creates a new column with loc.
Using iloc instead of loc with a boolean condition/column label.

steps.title: Clean data and rename columns
steps.instructions: Run `df.dropna()` and `df.fillna({'OrderID': 0}, inplace=True)`. Rename a column with `df.rename(columns={'OrderID': 'Order ID'}, inplace=True)` and display df.

targets.caption: Fill missing values in place
Rename a column and show df

explanations.topic: dropna removes rows with null/NA values
fillna replaces missing values instead of removing rows
inplace=True modifies the existing DataFrame instead of returning a new one
Renaming columns with df.rename

hints: Missing values can be dropped with one DataFrame method or filled with another; both end in 'na'.
Pass a dictionary of {column: fill_value} to fillna, and add inplace=True so df itself changes.
Rename with df.rename(columns={'OldName': 'New Name'}, inplace=True), then put df on the last line of a cell to display it.
Full code: df.fillna({'OrderID': 0}, inplace=True); df.rename(columns={'OrderID': 'Order ID'}, inplace=True); df
common_mistakes: Forgetting inplace=True (or not reassigning df = ...), so the rename or fill silently doesn't stick.
Passing the mapping directly as df.rename({'OrderID': 'Order ID'}) without columns=, which renames index labels instead of columns.
Misspelling the original column name (e.g. 'OrderId'). rename ignores missing keys, so nothing changes and no error is raised.
Running the rename cell twice and then using 'OrderID' in later cells, which raises a KeyError because the column is now 'Order ID'.
Expecting df.dropna() alone to change df. Without inplace=True it only returns a new DataFrame.

steps.title: Analyze, group and save data
steps.instructions: Run `df['Country'].value_counts()`, `df.groupby('Country')['Price'].sum()` and `df.sort_values('Price', ascending=False)`. Save with `df.to_csv('new_file.csv', index=False)`.

targets.caption: Count how often each country appears
Total price per country
Save the DataFrame to a new CSV

explanations.topic: value_counts counts each distinct value in a column
groupby works like SQL GROUP BY: sum price per country
sort_values with ascending=False sorts descending
to_csv index=True/False controls writing the index column

hints: Select a single column first, then call a counting method on it.
For grouping, use df.groupby('Country') and then select the 'Price' column before calling .sum().
sort_values takes the column name and ascending=False to put the most expensive rows first.
Save with df.to_csv('new_file.csv', index=False) and check that the file appears in your file browser.
common_mistakes: Calling value_counts on the whole DataFrame instead of on the 'Country' column.
Writing groupby('Country').sum()['Price'] on columns that are not numeric, which raises errors or gives unexpected results. Select ['Price'] before .sum().
Leaving Price as a string after cleaning, so the sum concatenates text or the sort is alphabetical.
Forgetting ascending=False, so the cheapest items appear first.
Omitting index=False, which writes an extra unnamed index column to the CSV.
Using to_csv without the underscore (tocsv), or misspelling the column name with the wrong case.
